body: The third Saturday running, a man is at the garden centre buying compost, the same three bags he has bought every spring for years. The woman at the till knows him well enough to ask after his wife, because she always asks after his wife, and he says she is well, thank you, and pays. His wife died in February. Correcting her would take eleven minutes and there are four people in the queue and a boy waiting to load the bags into the boot, so he does not correct her. He puts the compost in the car, gets in, and sits in the car park with the engine off for longer than he meant to.

He was not protecting the woman at the till. He was avoiding the reply. He knows its shape by heart now — the face, the hand on the forearm, the sentence about a better place — and he has decided that this morning he cannot carry another one of those.

Grief attracts solutions. Stages that suggest an itinerary. Reasons offered on God’s behalf. Reassurance about where the person is now. Practical suggestions, delivered early, about what might help. Almost none of it was asked for, and the grieving person can hear every bit of it coming.

There is a station on this dial that carries the subject and it is called Grief Walked, and the verb is doing the work. You can walk with somebody without knowing where they are going. You go at their pace rather than your own. You face the same direction, which means you are not looking at each other, which is exactly why people say the difficult thing on a walk and not across a table. Nobody announces a destination and nobody checks the time. Set that against the language we normally reach for — working through it, processing it, closure — all borrowed from engineering and administration, and all of it quietly promising an exit. Walking promises no exit at all. It promises a companion.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, of which 46 are on air today. Grief Walked holds HM 393.10. That number is assigned and the station is in build, and it is not yet on air — nothing plays there this afternoon.

Holding the number anyway is the expensive part. A frequency here belongs to one station permanently, so HM 393.10 sits reserved for a format that will never be popular, where something livelier could have gone. It is kept because the subject is not optional; sooner or later it is everybody. And the brief that station has been given is deliberately narrow. Do not move the listener along. Almost everything said to a grieving person is an attempt to make the sentence stop, and walking alongside is the one response that does not.

That is a strange brief now, because we have built a whole vocabulary for the opposite. Bereavement leave is counted in days. Sympathy has a half-life and most people can feel it expiring in the room. There are stages, which began as a description of something observed and became, in ordinary speech, a timetable with an end on it — so a person who is not on schedule starts to suspect they are grieving incorrectly. None of this is cruelty. It is what happens in a culture that is very good at fixing things and has almost no practice at accompanying them.

The book of Job is arranged to teach precisely this, and the arrangement is easy to miss because the part that works is so short. His friends hear what has happened, they travel, and when they see him from a distance they do not recognise him. They sit on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights and not one of them says a word, because they see that his grief is very great. That is the only stretch of the book where anybody gets it right.
They did not become wrong when their theology slipped. They became wrong the moment they started answering.

The therapeutic response deserves better than a caricature, and it should be said plainly that it works. Grief counselling helps people. A bereavement group in a church hall on a Wednesday evening is among the more useful things the Church quietly does. What none of it can do is be there on a Tuesday at four in the morning, which is when this is at its worst and least presentable. Appointments end. Groups meet fortnightly. The hours in between are the great majority of the hours, and they go unattended because no human arrangement can staff them.
Company is not treatment. It was never supposed to be.

A woman lets herself into her brother’s flat on a Sunday evening with a roll of bin bags under her arm, because the landlord wants it cleared by the end of the month. The flat has been shut up for five weeks and smells like it. She starts with the kitchen drawers, because starting anywhere else is impossible. At some point she props her phone against a mug on the windowsill and puts a station on, and it plays a trio, three women, something with a key change in it that she would have called dated if anybody had asked her. Nobody asks her. She works until midnight, fills nine bags, and sits down on the floor against the cupboard, and the thing she notices, when she notices anything, is that the entire evening has not cost her a single sentence.

Nothing in that room required an account of herself. That is the mechanism, and it is very small, and it is not available from anybody who loves her — because everybody who loves her, quite properly, wants to know how she is.

It should be said flatly that this does not help. A station will not make her brother less dead or the flat less empty, and some evenings it will make things worse, because a song will arrive that he liked and she will be ambushed in a stranger’s kitchen at half past ten. It cannot bring food round. It cannot come to the funeral. It does not know his name and it never will.

That is not a shortfall in the station. It is the qualification. Everything that offers to help is implying, underneath, that there is an end to be helped towards, and the grieving person hears that implication. A thing that offers nothing implies nothing. It simply keeps turning up at the same hour whether she is any better or not, which is what she would ask of a friend if she could bear to ask anybody for anything, and which is the one thing a published schedule can actually do.

So nothing here is going to fix it, and that is the offer. The dial does not know she is bereaved and cannot adjust to it, and both halves of that are the point. It will not lower its voice when she comes into the room. It will not look at her a little too carefully. It will not ask, kindly, how she has been sleeping. It is on. It was on before she found it. It will be on long after she stops needing it, and it will not notice that either.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial carries four kinds of programming — music, which is most of it; teaching and prayer; family programming; and the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated afterwards. There is a whole quiet corner built for hours like these, and most of it is still being built: Grief Walked at HM 393.10, Walking Together at HM 397.60, Stillwater at HM 365.40, all assigned, all in build, none of them yet on air. Until they open, the honest advice is the less obvious one, and it is the thing people get wrong: what you want in an empty flat is not a station about grief.

Put on HM 301.90 — Radiant Stones Concerts. It is on air now. It is a trio station, female voices in three-part harmony, the Sandi Patty and Avalon tradition brought forward, and it is not remotely a grief format. That is precisely why it is the recommendation. It has no idea what has happened in your house and it will not modulate for you. And harmony is company made audible: a trio cannot sing a solo, and three voices holding a chord is the sound of a room with more than one person in it, which is the sound an empty flat is missing at ten at night. It is warm without being interested in you, and on the evening you are filling bin bags it is worth more than sympathy.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — the site is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. Add the page to your home screen if you like. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are reaching for at four in the morning — which is how the quiet corner of the dial gets built, and Grief Walked with it.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer, because nothing is being promised. Do not try it and see whether it works. Working is the thing it does not do. Put HM 301.90 on this evening while you are doing something with your hands, and then leave it alone. Let it play whether or not you chose. It will not fix one single thing, it will not ask you anything, and it will still be there tomorrow at the same hour, going at your pace, headed nowhere in particular.
